conventional_description: In Western medicine, chronic pelvic pain is defined as pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis that persists for at least six months, not exclusively related to menstruation or intercourse. It can stem from many sources, including endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, irritable bowel syndrome, interstitial cystitis, or musculoskeletal issues. Diagnosis often involves a combination of imaging (ultrasound, MRI), laparoscopy, and ruling out other conditions. Because the cause can be complex, treatment is often multidisciplinary, yet many women continue to suffer despite exhaustive workups.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain, hormonal therapies (birth control pills, GnRH agonists) for endometriosis-related pain, physical therapy for pelvic floor dysfunction, and sometimes nerve blocks. In refractory cases, surgery such as laparoscopic excision of endometriosis or hysterectomy may be offered. Psychological support and cognitive behavioral therapy are also recommended to help cope with chronic pain.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands chronic pelvic pain primarily through the lens of the Liver, Spleen, and Kidney organ systems, and the flow of Qi and Blood in the lower burner (the pelvic region). The Liver is responsible for the smooth movement of Qi throughout the body, and emotional stress, frustration, or unresolved anger can cause Liver Qi to stagnate. Over time, stagnant Qi fails to move Blood, leading to fixed, stabbing pain - the hallmark of Qi and Blood Stagnation.
The Spleen transforms food into Qi and Blood and manages the body's fluids. When the Spleen is weakened by poor diet, overwork, or worry, it fails to process dampness, which then accumulates and sinks downward. If dampness combines with heat (from spicy foods, alcohol, or stress), it creates a burning, heavy pain with thick discharge - Damp-Heat.
If dampness combines with cold (from exposure to cold environments or internal yang deficiency), it creates a cold, heavy ache that feels better with warmth - Cold-Dampness.
The Kidney provides the body's fundamental warming fire. When Kidney Yang is deficient, the pelvis lacks warmth, and cold congeals, causing a dull, persistent ache with lower back soreness and a sensation of cold. In some women, chronic illness or heavy menstrual blood loss depletes both Qi and Blood, so the pelvic organs are undernourished, leading to a dull ache that worsens with fatigue.
Because the same Western diagnosis can arise from such different root imbalances, TCM practitioners carefully differentiate the pattern based on the quality of pain, accompanying symptoms, tongue appearance, and pulse quality. This is why two women with 'chronic pelvic pain' might receive completely different herbal formulas - and why treatment can be so precisely targeted.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the quality of the pain-is it stabbing, burning, dull, or heavy? They also note what makes it better or worse, the timing in the menstrual cycle, and any accompanying symptoms like discharge, fatigue, or mood changes. These clues, together with tongue and pulse examination, narrow down the pattern.
If the pain is fixed, stabbing, and worse before or during the period, with dark clots and emotional stress, Qi and Blood Stagnation is likely. The tongue often looks purplish with dark spots, and the pulse feels wiry.
When the pain is burning and heavy, with thick yellow vaginal discharge or urinary discomfort, Damp-Heat has settled in the lower burner. The tongue appears red with a greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery.
Cold-Dampness produces a cold, heavy ache that worsens in cold or damp weather and improves with a heating pad. The tongue is pale with a white coating, and the pulse is deep and tight.
Chronic dull pain with a cold sensation and lower back soreness points to Kidney Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale and moist, and the pulse is deep and weak.
If the pain is a persistent dull ache that gets worse with overwork, and the person looks pale with scanty periods, Qi and Blood Deficiency is the culprit. The tongue is pale with a thin coating, and the pulse is weak and thready.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing lower abdominal pain", "Pain worsens with pressure", "Dark, clotted menstrual blood", "Premenstrual worsening of pain", "Irritability and mood swings", "Chest or breast distension"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress and frustration, Cold, raw foods and iced drinks, Prolonged sitting or inactivity, Cold, damp weather, Before and during menstruation
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement (walking, yoga), Warm compress on the lower abdomen, Stress reduction and relaxation, Light, easily digestible meals
patterns.why_this_happens: Chronic pelvic pain often begins when emotional stress, frustration, or unresolved anger cause the Liver Qi to knot up instead of flowing smoothly. Over time, that stagnant Qi can no longer push Blood through the pelvic vessels, and Blood stasis settles into the lower abdomen. This creates a fixed, stabbing pain that feels deep and relentless, flaring whenever pressure builds - especially before or during menstruation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dark body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress is the primary trigger because it directly knots the Liver Qi, and stagnant Qi soon leads to Blood stasis in the pelvis. Cold and inactivity further congeal Blood, making the pain sharper and more fixed. Menstruation naturally involves a downward movement of Blood, and when stasis is present, that flow becomes painful. Relief comes from warmth and gentle movement, which help unblock Qi and Blood, while stress reduction eases the Liver so the root cause of stagnation is calmed.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement like walking, yoga, or tai chi keeps Qi and Blood flowing - avoid long periods of sitting. Eat lightly and avoid cold, raw foods that congeal Blood; instead favor warming dishes with turmeric, ginger, and a little black pepper. Manage stress with deep breathing or meditation to prevent Liver Qi from stagnating again.

patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat are two pathological factors that can sink downward into the pelvis. Dampness is heavy and sticky, while Heat creates a burning sensation-together they cause a sensation of heaviness and burning pain deep in the lower abdomen. The Heat component also stirs up foul-smelling discharges and urinary urgency, while the Dampness makes the pain feel dragging and constant.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, slightly swollen, with a thick yellow greasy coating that is most prominent at the root. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò), often soggy (濡 rú) and strongest at the rear (Chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is like a sticky, hot swamp in the body. Spicy and greasy foods, alcohol, and hot weather add more Heat and Dampness, making the swamp worse. Cooling, drying habits-like light meals and gentle movement-help drain the swamp. Stress stirs up Liver Qi which can turn into Heat, so staying calm keeps the fire from flaring. Warm sitz baths soothe the area without adding more Heat, while a cool, dry environment prevents external Dampness from invading.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol-these all generate Damp-Heat. Favour cooling, damp-draining foods like mung beans, celery, barley, and cucumber. Keep the pelvic area clean and dry, avoid prolonged sitting, and choose gentle exercise like walking or yoga to encourage the smooth flow of Qi and fluids.

patterns.better_with: Heat packs on the lower abdomen, Warm drinks like ginger tea, Rest in a warm, dry environment, Moxibustion (heat therapy)
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's warming Yang energy is insufficient, external cold and dampness can invade the lower burner, or internal dampness from weak Spleen function can combine with cold. This heavy, congealing energy settles in the pelvis, obstructing the flow of Qi and Blood. The result is a persistent, dull, cold ache that feels heavy and dragging, much like cold water pooling in the lower abdomen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with tooth marks, thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: deep, slow, and soggy, especially in the rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are heavy, congealing energies that obstruct the flow of Qi and Blood. Heat and dryness directly oppose them, melting the cold away and drying up the dampness. Rest allows the body's Yang energy to consolidate, while overwork and cold exposure further deplete it, allowing cold-dampness to settle more deeply.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower abdomen and feet warm, and avoid sitting on cold surfaces. Eat warming foods like ginger, cinnamon, and lamb, while steering clear of raw, cold, or greasy foods that promote dampness. Gentle moxibustion on the lower belly can be a powerful home remedy.

patterns.better_with: Warmth (hot water bottle, warm bath), Warm, cooked foods and spices, Gentle movement (walking, tai chi), Rest and sleep, Moxibustion on lower abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidney's Yang is like the body's internal furnace, warming the uterus and lower abdomen. When this fire weakens, cold settles in the pelvis, causing a persistent dull ache and a sensation of cold. Without enough warmth, blood and Qi move sluggishly, leading to chronic pain that feels better with heat and pressure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender with teeth marks, wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the chi positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's source of warmth. Cold depletes it further, causing the pain to worsen, while warmth supports and restores it, easing the ache. Rest conserves Yang energy, and overwork drains it, so balancing activity with rest is crucial. Warm foods and moxibustion directly add heat to the system, helping to expel the internal cold that underlies the pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower abdomen and feet warm; a hot water bottle or warm bath can help. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and include warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and cloves. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi supports Yang, but avoid overexertion. Ensure adequate rest and sleep to conserve Kidney energy.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with chronic pelvic pain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can reduce pelvic pain by promoting the flow of Qi and Blood, relaxing pelvic floor muscles, and reducing inflammation. Many women find relief after a few sessions, especially when combined with Chinese herbs. The key is matching the treatment to your specific TCM pattern.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: For chronic conditions, a typical course is 6-12 weekly sessions, with progress evaluated every 4 weeks. Some women notice improvement after 2-3 sessions, but deeper patterns may require more time. Your practitioner will adjust frequency as your pain improves.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my pain medication or hormone therapy?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Acupuncture and many herbs are safe to combine with conventional treatments. However, some Chinese herbs that move Blood (such as Dang Gui or Tao Ren) may interact with blood thinners. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you are taking. Never stop prescribed medications abruptly.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a supportive role. In general, TCM recommends avoiding cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can worsen pelvic pain from cold or dampness. Focus on warm, cooked meals, and limit greasy, spicy, or overly sweet foods that generate dampness and heat. Your practitioner may give more specific advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe if I'm trying to conceive?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is often used to support fertility and can be safely integrated while trying to conceive. Many herbal formulas are used to regulate the menstrual cycle and improve pelvic health. However, if you are actively undergoing fertility treatments, inform your TCM practitioner so they can adjust herbs accordingly.

faqs.question: Does TCM treat the root cause or just the pain?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to treat the root imbalance causing the pain, not just mask the symptom. For example, if your pain is due to Liver Qi stagnation, the herbs and acupuncture points will smooth the flow of Qi and address emotional stress, so pain diminishes naturally. This approach often leads to lasting relief and fewer recurrences.

faqs.question: What if my pain is caused by endometriosis?
faqs.answer: In TCM, endometriosis is seen as a form of Blood Stagnation, often with underlying Qi stagnation or Cold. The herbs and acupuncture points used will be chosen based on your individual pattern - not just the Western diagnosis. Many women with endometriosis find that TCM reduces pain and improves quality of life, even if the endometrial tissue remains.

faqs.question: Will the results last after I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: When the root imbalance is corrected, results can be long-lasting. However, lifestyle factors (stress, diet, exposure to cold) can cause a recurrence. Your practitioner will guide you on how to maintain balance, and occasional 'tune-up' sessions may be helpful.

research.title: Cai's gynecology chronic pelvic formula combined with conventional therapy for chronic pelvic pain: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This randomized controlled trial evaluated the addition of Cai's gynecology chronic pelvic formula - a TCM herbal prescription targeting Qi and Blood stagnation with dampness - to standard biomedical treatment for chronic pelvic pain. The herbal group showed significantly greater reductions in pain intensity and improvements in quality of life compared to the control group receiving conventional therapy alone. The formula was well-tolerated with no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Wang L, et al. Cai's gynecology chronic pelvic formula combined with conventional therapy for chronic pelvic pain: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Transl Res. 2024;17(7):4470-4482.
